                                     PERSONAL INFORMATION

Q. Please state your name and address.
A. My name is Krista Harris. I am also identified in the official records of the McCulloch County
Appraisal District as Krista Demar Reynolds. My address is in McCulloch County, Texas, on the parcel
identified by the Applicants on the publicly filed Link H3 map as Tract 68789.

Q. Are you an intervenor in this proceeding? If so, please explain how.
A. Yes. I am an individually intervening landowner in PUC Docket No. 59475 and SOAH Docket No.
473-26-16349. I am the owner of record of the parcel identified on the Applicants' publicly filed maps as
Tract 68789, located in McCulloch County, Texas. The proposed H3 link is drawn directly across and
perpendicular to the front of my home. Other proposed links in the study area — including the I1 link to
the southwest of my property, the G6 link running east-west south of my property, and the G44 link
(formerly identified as G4) running perpendicular to the I1 and G6 — are in the vicinity but it is the H3
that physically crosses my parcel and passes immediately in front of my habitable home.

Q. Please state your familiarity with the property.
A. I am the owner of record and a resident of the property. I have direct, personal knowledge of its current
condition, its terrain, its native vegetation, the location of my residence and other improvements, the
drives and access points, the wildlife that uses the land, the historic use of the property, and the seasonal
weather and flooding patterns. I have walked, worked, and lived on this land and am fully familiar with
every feature relevant to this proceeding.

Q. Are you testifying on your own or on behalf of another entity?
A. I am testifying solely on my own behalf as the individual landowner of Tract 68789. I am not
testifying on behalf of any company, organization, group, association, fund, or other entity. This is my
personal testimony as the person who lives on and owns this land.

Q. What is the purpose of your testimony?
A. The purpose of my testimony is to demonstrate that the proposed H3 segment of the Bell County East
Switch to Big Hill 765-kV transmission line, as drawn perpendicular to and in front of my home on Tract
68789, is incompatible with the criteria the Commission must consider under the Public Utility
Regulatory Act (PURA), the Texas Utilities Code, and the Commission's routing rule at 16 TAC §
25.101. The H3 alignment as drawn fails the statutory directive to give due consideration to community
values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and land use
compatibility under PURA § 37.056(c). It also fails the prudent-avoidance principle embodied in PURA §
37.056(c)(4)(D) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), and it fails the Commission's longstanding preference for
paralleling existing compatible rights-of-way and avoiding habitable structures.

Q. What is your overall concern with the proposed routing across your property?


Direct Testimony of Krista Harris
PUC Docket No. 59475

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

                                                                                                 Page 4 of 22
 A. My primary concerns are that the H3 link as drawn perpendicular to the front of my home: (1) places
the proposed centerline and its associated 200-foot easement and 500-foot prudent-avoidance setback
envelope immediately in front of, and within striking distance of, my habitable residence; (2) does not
parallel or co-locate with the existing constructed compatible electric transmission infrastructure already
depicted on the same parcel and along the corridor of record, in direct conflict with 16 TAC §
25.101(b)(3)(B)(ii); (3) bisects the working, residential, and most actively used portions of my land; (4)
destroys the rural, quiet, scenic character that defines both my homestead and the surrounding
community; (5) introduces unmitigated visual, auditory (corona), and electromagnetic intrusion on a full-
time occupied dwelling; (6) fragments wildlife habitat and disturbs the native ecosystem that I have
protected and stewarded; and (7) measurably and permanently diminishes the market value of my
property. None of these harms are necessary, because the Applicants had compatible existing alignments
available to them and chose instead to draw H3 across the front of my home.

Q. Have you ever testified at the Public Utility Commission of Texas before?
A. No. This is my first time providing testimony before the Commission.

Q. Was this material prepared by you or under your supervision?
A. Yes. I prepared this testimony myself, drawing on my own personal knowledge of my property, my
review of the Applicants' publicly filed Link H3 map, and my review of the applicable statutory and
regulatory framework.




Direct Testimony of Krista Harris
PUC Docket No. 59475

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

                                                                                                Page 5 of 22
                           PROPERTY DESCRIPTION AND LOCATION

Q. Please describe your property.
A. My property is the parcel identified on the Applicants' publicly filed Link H3 map as Tract 68789 in
McCulloch County, Texas. It is further identified in the official records of the McCulloch County
Appraisal District under my recorded name, Krista Demar Reynolds. The parcel is rural land typical of
the Edwards Plateau / Hill Country terrain in McCulloch County. It contains my full-time residence and
the improvements associated with rural homestead and ranch use. The terrain consists of rolling hills with
thin caliche-and-limestone soils over fractured rock, supporting native Hill Country vegetation and
wildlife. The Permian-Katy "P2K" Pipeline System alignment of record crosses the northern portion of
the property area, and existing compatible transmission infrastructure follows established corridors in the
vicinity. The proposed H3 centerline is drawn perpendicular to and directly across the front of my home.

Q. How is access to the property obtained?
A. Access to my property is obtained from the public roadway via a long-established driveway and access
route that approaches the home from the road frontage. Because the H3 centerline is drawn perpendicular
to the front of the home, the access drive and the area my family and every visitor, service provider, and
emergency responder uses to reach the home falls inside the H3 impact envelope. There are no alternative
improved access routes.

Q. Do you have pictures or exhibits that support your description of your property?
A. Yes. I have attached, or am prepared to attach, dated photographs and a copy of the relevant portion of
the Applicants' publicly filed Link H3 map sheet that depicts Tract 68789. The map clearly shows the H3
centerline crossing perpendicular to the front of my home, the I1 link located southwest of my property,
the G6 link running east-west south of my property, the G44 link (formerly G4) running perpendicular to
both I1 and G6 at their intersection south of my property, and the P2K pipeline alignment of record
crossing the northern portion of the area. The photographs accurately and fairly depict the property as of
the dates listed, and the condition of the property has not materially changed since the dates the
photographs were taken.

Q. Where is your property located relative to the proposed routes?
A. My property — Tract 68789 — is located such that the proposed H3 link is drawn directly across it,
running perpendicular to the front of my home. In the current configuration depicted on the Applicants'
map: the I1 link runs to the southwest of my property; the G6 link runs east-west south of my property;
and the G44 link (formerly identified as G4) runs perpendicular to the I1 and G6, intersecting them south
of my property. Critically, the G44 (formerly G4) does not run alongside my home as it once did in earlier
route iterations. The route immediately and directly impacting my home and homestead in the current
configuration is the H3.

Q. Which routes affect your property?


Direct Testimony of Krista Harris
PUC Docket No. 59475

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

                                                                                                Page 6 of 22
 A. The H3 link is the route that directly crosses my property and is drawn perpendicular to and
immediately in front of my home. The I1, G6, and G44 links are in the vicinity of my property — the I1
to the southwest, the G6 east-west south of the property, and the G44 perpendicular to both I1 and G6 —
but none of those three runs across my home or its habitable curtilage in the current configuration. The
H3 is the link that imposes the direct, severe, and statutorily disqualifying impact on my parcel.

Q. What routes do you oppose or support?
A. I oppose every macro-route that incorporates the H3 link as currently drawn across Tract 68789. For
the reasons explained throughout this testimony, no route that includes the H3 alignment as drawn can
satisfy the statutory criteria of PURA § 37.056(c) or the Commission's routing rule at 16 TAC §
25.101(b)(3)(B), because it places a 765-kV transmission centerline perpendicular to and directly in front
of an occupied habitable structure, fails to parallel existing compatible rights-of-way, and disregards the
prudent-avoidance principle the Commission is required to apply.




Direct Testimony of Krista Harris
PUC Docket No. 59475

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

                                                                                                Page 7 of 22
                                     LAND USE AND HISTORY

Q. Please describe the history of your property and your association with it.
A. This property has been the place I have made my home and the land I have tended and protected. It is
the place where my family lives, where we make our daily life, and where we plan our future. My
association with the property is not abstract or commercial — it is the home I wake up in, the land I walk
every day, and the heritage I intend to pass on. The land lies in a part of McCulloch County that has been
rural ranch country for generations, and my use of the property is consistent with that historic and
ongoing community character.

Q. How is the property currently used?
A. The property is my full-time residence and is used for rural homestead and land-management activities
consistent with the surrounding McCulloch County community. I steward the native Hill Country habitat,
maintain the home and its surrounding improvements, and use the working portions of the property in a
manner consistent with rural and agricultural values. The home is occupied year-round, and the area in
front of the home — through which the H3 centerline is drawn perpendicular — is the approach, view,
and daily-use area of my residence.

Q. How would the proposed transmission line affect your use of the property?
A. The proposed H3 centerline as drawn would impose a 200-foot permanent easement and a 500-foot
prudent-avoidance setback envelope running perpendicular to the front of my home. This would: (i) place
ultra-high-voltage 765-kV structures and conductors directly across the approach and front view of my
full-time residence; (ii) place my home inside the regulatory prudent-avoidance envelope established
under the Commission's longstanding interpretation of PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(D); (iii) impair or eliminate
the safe use of normal residential and ranch equipment in the affected area; (iv) introduce ongoing utility
access, audible corona noise, and visual intrusion across the heart of my homestead; (v) create temporary
construction areas, access roads, and staging zones that are not even shown on the Applicants' published
maps, which would compound the damage; and (vi) permanently change the character, usefulness, and
value of the home I live in. None of these impacts is necessary, because the H3 alignment could have
been drawn to parallel existing compatible infrastructure and avoid habitable structures, as the
Commission's rules require.




Direct Testimony of Krista Harris
PUC Docket No. 59475

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

                                                                                                Page 8 of 22
                            COMMUNITY VALUES AND AESTHETICS

Q. How does your property contribute to community values?
A. My property is part of the quiet, rural, agricultural and ranching character of McCulloch County. The
area is defined by large open tracts, native vegetation, dark skies, low ambient noise, and neighborly self-
reliance. My use of the property — as a full-time home in keeping with surrounding rural use — fits
squarely within and reinforces that community character. PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A) requires the
Commission to consider community values, and the community value in this part of McCulloch County is
rural, quiet, and unindustrialized.

Q. How important are views and visual character to your property?
A. The views from my home and from the working portions of my property are central to the meaning,
enjoyment, and value of the land. The view from the front of my home — the very area through which the
H3 centerline is drawn perpendicular — is part of what makes this place my home and not just a parcel of
dirt. The natural horizon, native vegetation, and open sky that define the front view of my home are
exactly the kind of aesthetic values PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C) directs the Commission to consider.

Q. How would the transmission line affect the aforementioned values?
A. A 765-kV transmission line with the required tall structures and a 200-foot cleared right-of-way,
running perpendicular to and directly across the front of my home, would permanently and irreversibly
destroy the quiet rural character, the views, the night skies, and the aesthetic integrity that give this
property and this part of McCulloch County its identity. The visual, auditory (corona hum), and industrial
presence would be fundamentally incompatible with the existing community values and aesthetic values
that PURA § 37.056(c) directs the Commission to protect and the Commission's routing rule at 16 TAC §
25.101(b)(3)(B) requires the Commission to weigh.




Direct Testimony of Krista Harris
PUC Docket No. 59475

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

                                                                                                Page 9 of 22
                           HISTORICAL AND CULTURAL RESOURCES

Q. Are there any archaeological sites or artifacts?
A. The portion of McCulloch County in which my property lies is within a broader landscape that has
been inhabited and traversed for centuries. Artifacts of historic and prehistoric use are commonly found
on rural properties throughout the region. To the extent any such items, scatters, or features exist on the
property, they would lie within the 200-foot easement, the 500-foot setback envelope, or the unshown
temporary construction and access areas associated with the H3 link as drawn — and would be at direct
risk of disturbance.

Q. Are there any historic structures or historically significant features?
A. The home, improvements, and rural-landscape features on the property are part of the historic rural and
ranching character of McCulloch County. My residence is an inhabited historic-character homestead in
the McCulloch County rural fabric. Drawing a 765-kV transmission alignment perpendicular to and
across the front of such a structure is fundamentally inconsistent with the protection of historic and
aesthetic values the Commission is directed to consider under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C).

Q. How would the proposed routes affecting your property impact these resources?
A. Any historic, cultural, or archaeological features located within the 200-foot easement, the 500-foot
prudent-avoidance envelope, or any temporary construction or access areas would be at direct risk of
disturbance, damage, or destruction during construction and ongoing maintenance of the H3 line. The
visual setting of my home — itself a historic-character feature — would be permanently altered. These
impacts implicate PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C) and the Antiquities Code framework reflected in Texas
Natural Resources Code, Title 9, Chapter 191, which require careful assessment before industrial
development is permitted to alter or destroy cultural-resource settings.




Direct Testimony of Krista Harris
PUC Docket No. 59475

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

                                                                                                Page 10 of 22
                                     ENVIRONMENTAL INTEGRITY

Q. Are there environmentally sensitive areas on your property?
A. Yes. My property supports the native Hill Country / Edwards Plateau wildlife and vegetative
community typical of McCulloch County, including native deer, turkey, songbirds, raptors, pollinators,
native grasses and forbs, and smaller mammals and reptiles. The wooded and pasture areas provide
habitat connectivity that would be fragmented by the H3 cleared corridor cutting perpendicular across the
front of the home and through the working areas of the parcel. Native bunch grasses, mealy blue sage,
cenizo, flame acanthus, and similar Hill Country flora support pollinators and ground-nesting birds whose
populations are already in regional decline.

Q. Are there soils, slopes, or terrain features that present environmental risk?
A. Yes. The terrain on and around my property is rolling Hill Country with thin caliche-and-limestone
soils over fractured-rock substrate. Surface runoff during precipitation events is relatively rapid, with
limited natural retention capacity. Slopes, drainage features, and thin soil profiles characteristic of the
Edwards Plateau make this landscape unusually vulnerable to construction disturbance, compaction, and
accelerated erosion.

Q. How would the project impact environmental conditions on your property?
A. Clearing mature vegetation for the H3 corridor, combined with heavy-equipment compaction across
thin Hill Country soils, would: (i) increase wind-loading on remaining trees and vegetation; (ii) expose
thin soils to direct rainfall and accelerate erosion; (iii) fragment wildlife habitat and disrupt native
pollinator and ground-nesting communities; (iv) introduce sediment and potential fluid releases into the
local watershed; and (v) introduce electromagnetic and corona effects that scientific literature has linked
to navigation confusion and reduced foraging in pollinators and to aversive effects on bats. These impacts
directly implicate the environmental-integrity factor the Commission must weigh under PURA §
37.056(c)(4)(B) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(iv).




Direct Testimony of Krista Harris
PUC Docket No. 59475

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

                                                                                                Page 11 of 22
                               WATER RESOURCES AND FLOODING

Q. Have you observed flooding on your property?
A. McCulloch County and the surrounding Hill Country are well-known for rapid runoff and flash-flood
behavior during precipitation events, given the thin soils and fractured-rock substrate. I have personally
observed water moving quickly across the landscape during heavy rains, and roads and low-water
crossings in this part of the county are subject to washout. Heavy construction and clearing along the H3
corridor would worsen these conditions immediately upstream and across from my home.

Q. Are there creeks, springs, wetlands, or seeps present?
A. The drainages, wet-weather draws, and intermittent water features typical of Hill Country properties
are present in the area in and around my parcel. These features collect, channel, and convey rainfall across
the landscape and are sensitive to upstream disturbance, sediment loading, and compaction caused by the
kind of industrial construction the H3 link would require.

Q. How do you think construction for this type of project could impact drainage or flooding?
A. Heavy-equipment work, grading, soil compaction, and clearing of stabilizing vegetation across the
200-foot H3 easement (and across any unshown temporary construction and staging areas) would increase
the velocity and volume of surface runoff, generate sediment loads, and create new pathways for
incidental hydrocarbon or fluid releases into the local hydrologic system. Because the H3 centerline is
drawn perpendicular to the front of my home, any altered drainage or concentrated runoff caused by
construction would tend to be directed toward or across the most actively used portions of my homestead.
This is precisely the type of avoidable impact the prudent-avoidance principle directs the Commission to
weigh.




Direct Testimony of Krista Harris
PUC Docket No. 59475

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

                                                                                               Page 12 of 22
                              WATER SUPPLY AND GROUNDWATER

Q. Do you rely on groundwater wells?
A. Yes. Like the rural homesteads around me in McCulloch County, my property relies on groundwater
for domestic and household use. The Hickory Sandstone and Ellenburger–San Saba aquifers underlie the
area, and McCulloch County lies within the jurisdiction of the Hickory Underground Water Conservation
District No. 1. Any disturbance to the geology or the surface adjacent to a well introduces direct risk to
the well and the household it serves.

Q. Are there stock ponds or stock tanks on the property?
A. The property and its surrounding area contain the kinds of small water-retention features and tanks
typical of Hill Country rural property use. Heavy-equipment construction in and across the H3 corridor
would create direct risk to these features through compaction, sediment loading, and altered drainage.

Q. What risks do you anticipate this project could pose to your water supply?
A. Tower foundation installation — particularly the rock drilling, blasting, or anchoring required in
fractured-limestone Hill Country geology — would introduce vibration, ground-loading, and fluid-release
risk (drilling muds, hydraulic fluid, fuel) directly into or near the wellhead and annulus of any nearby
domestic well. For any uncased or partially cased well, those impacts can propagate into the producing
zone. Even properly cased wells face physical-damage risk during the construction window. Because the
H3 centerline is drawn perpendicular to and across the front of my home, construction activity will occur
in immediate proximity to my domestic water supply.




Direct Testimony of Krista Harris
PUC Docket No. 59475

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

                                                                                              Page 13 of 22
                                     AGRICULTURAL OPERATIONS

Q. What agricultural or land management activities occur on your property?
A. The property is managed in a manner consistent with rural McCulloch County land use. I maintain
native vegetation and habitat suitable for the wildlife typical of the Hill Country, manage the working
areas of the parcel for the kind of rural and agricultural use customary to the region, and steward the land
for long-term productivity and habitability. The McCulloch County Appraisal District's productivity-
valuation framework reflects this rural use.

Q. Are there seasonal operations, such as calving, harvesting, and/or hunting?
A. The property and its surrounding landscape support the seasonal cycles of native wildlife — fawning,
nesting, breeding, and migration — and the customary rural-use cycles of the McCulloch County
ranching community. These cycles are sensitive to noise, vibration, lighting, dust, and human-and-
equipment traffic of the kind the H3 construction would impose perpendicular to my home.

Q. How would construction interfere with these operations?
A. Construction noise, vibration, lighting, dust, and heavy-equipment traffic — concentrated
perpendicular to and directly across the front of my home — would interrupt fawning and nesting cycles,
disturb wildlife movement patterns, and disrupt the customary rural and agricultural use of the property.
The permanent cleared 200-foot corridor and the steel structures and conductors of a 765-kV line would
fragment wildlife movement and permanently alter animal behavior across the parcel. These impacts
directly affect agricultural and rural land use under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(B).




Direct Testimony of Krista Harris
PUC Docket No. 59475

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

                                                                                                Page 14 of 22
                     ENGINEERING, ACCESS, AND CONSTRUCTABILITY

Q. Are there limitations to accessing your property?
A. Yes. My property is accessed from the public roadway via a long-established drive and access route
that approaches the home from the front — the very area through which the H3 centerline is drawn
perpendicular. There is no alternative improved access. Construction of an ultra-high-voltage line across
the front approach to the home would interfere with that access during the construction window and
would impose permanent utility-maintenance access burdens across the approach to my residence.

Q. Are there terrain or soil constraints?
A. Yes. The Hill Country terrain on and around my property features thin caliche-and-limestone soils
over fractured rock. Tower foundations of the size required for 765-kV structures require deep drilling,
rock anchoring, or blasting in this geology. These soils and substrates are also unstable when disturbed
and compacted, and they are vulnerable to erosion once stabilizing vegetation is cleared.

Q. Are there conflicts with existing infrastructure?
A. Yes. The H3 centerline as drawn does not parallel or co-locate with existing compatible electric
transmission corridors in the area, and it crosses the Permian-Katy "P2K" Pipeline System alignment of
record. The Applicants' map shows the P2K alignment running east-west across the northern portion of
the area, the I1 link to the southwest of my property, the G6 link running east-west south of my property,
and the G44 link (formerly G4) running perpendicular to the I1 and G6. Rather than utilizing or
paralleling the existing utility corridors and links available, the H3 alignment cuts a new path
perpendicular to the front of my home. This conflicts with the Commission's longstanding routing
preference, codified at 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(ii), for paralleling existing compatible rights-of-way.

Q. How do you think the soil constraints and existing infrastructure could affect the construction,
maintenance, or safety of these lines?
A. Thin Hill Country soils over fractured limestone create heightened construction risk: deep rock drilling
and anchoring of large 765-kV tower foundations generate vibration, dust, and the potential for fluid
releases that can propagate through fractured substrate. Once vegetation is cleared, the same thin soils
erode rapidly under rainfall and wind. The presence of the P2K pipeline alignment of record in the same
area introduces additional engineering and safety considerations that the H3 alignment as drawn does not
address. None of these risks is acceptable when the H3 centerline is drawn perpendicular to and
immediately in front of an occupied habitable home, and when compatible existing corridors were
available to be paralleled.




Direct Testimony of Krista Harris
PUC Docket No. 59475

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

                                                                                              Page 15 of 22
                  PRUDENT AVOIDANCE AND HABITABLE STRUCTURES

Q. Please describe all habitable structures on your property.
A. My property contains my full-time residence — a habitable home, occupied year-round by me and my
family. This is not a hunting cabin, a recreational structure, or an occasional-use building. It is my
primary, daily, full-time dwelling. The home is located on the parcel such that the proposed H3 centerline
is drawn perpendicular to and directly across its front, with the home and its curtilage falling within the
500-foot prudent-avoidance setback envelope associated with a 765-kV line.

Q. Are there any habitable structures within 500 feet of the proposed centerline?
A. Yes. My full-time residence is within the 500-foot setback envelope of the H3 centerline as drawn. The
Applicants' publicly filed Link H3 map appears to depict the H3 centerline crossing the parcel
perpendicular to the front of the home without adequately accounting for the home as a habitable structure
within the setback envelope. Any failure to depict my residence as a habitable structure within the H3
setback is itself a record-accuracy concern the Commission must address, because the Commission's
longstanding interpretation of PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(D) requires identification of and prudent avoidance
around habitable structures.

Q. Beyond the home itself, are there outdoor living areas, ranch structures, or work areas affected
by the proposed centerline?
A. Yes. The area in front of the home — the approach, the front view, the daily-use yard, and the working
approach to the residence — falls directly within the H3 centerline's 200-foot easement and its 500-foot
setback envelope. The portions of the parcel through which I and any visitor, service provider, or
emergency responder must pass to reach the home are entirely within the H3 impact footprint. The G44
link (formerly G4) does not run alongside my home as it once did in earlier configurations, the G6 link
runs east-west south of my property, and the I1 link runs to the southwest of my property; none of those
three crosses the active living and working area in front of the home. The H3 is the link that does.

Q. How close are the proposed routes to these structures?
A. The H3 centerline is drawn perpendicular to and directly in front of my home, with the home and its
curtilage falling within the 500-foot prudent-avoidance setback envelope. The other proposed links in the
vicinity — I1 (to the southwest), G6 (east-west south of the property), and G44 (formerly G4, running
perpendicular to I1 and G6) — are in the area but do not impose the close-proximity impact on my home
that the H3 does.

Q. What areas of your property are most actively used?
A. The most actively used area of my property is my home and the area in front of and immediately
around the home — the approach, the front yard, the access drive, the daily-living curtilage. That is the
precise area through which the H3 centerline is drawn perpendicular and within whose 500-foot setback
the residence sits.


Direct Testimony of Krista Harris
PUC Docket No. 59475

SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

                                                                                              Page 16 of 22
 Q. Does the current route placement require you to move any existing structures or hinder your
ability to build planned structures?
A. Yes. The 200-foot H3 easement and the 500-foot prudent-avoidance setback envelope foreclose the
placement of any new improvements, outbuildings, cross-fencing, or additions in the affected area in front
of my home, and they place ongoing utility-access burdens across my approach. The presence of an active
